source: Strand, Richard F. Transcription and Pronunciation of the Nûristânî Languages. Richard Strand's Nuristân Site.
claim: Strand states that Kâmviri (K.km) data were collected by him in the field and that phonemic analysis of the K.km raw field data is complete; Kâtâ-vari dialect data have varying source and analysis status.
lect_scope: Kâmviri, with comparative Kâmkata-vari dialect evidence where explicitly labelled

claim: Strand's transcription is explicitly phonemic and minimizes predictable articulatory marking; actual phones are separately bracketed, so database extraction must not inflate predictable surface realizations into phonemes.

In Kâmkata-vari, consonant sequences containing obstruents, or obstruents plus a nasal stop, are uniformly voiced or voiceless; voicing is anticipatory and determined by the final obstruent or nasal in the sequence.
The default vowel a is [ɨ] in Kâmkata-vari and is fronted to [i] after lamino-alveolar consonants; â is a contrasting open central [a].
Strand states that Kâmkata-vari /u/ derives historically from earlier /o/ and /au/, contrasting its history with Ashkun u from Indo-Iranian *u.
Front rounded /ü/ occurs in Kâmviri and Eastern Kâtâ-vari, but in Ktivi Kâtâ-vari it has lost phonemic distinctiveness through dissimilation to /iu/.
Kâmviri å [ɒ~ɔ] is described as marginally phonemic and used to represent Dari/Farsi â in loanwords.
Nasalized vowels occur in Kâmviri and are attributed to reduction of ancient *n; the comparative source notes loss of nasalized vowels in one Kâtâ-vari dialect (K.ktw).
Vowel length is distinctive in Kâmviri; Strand illustrates a lexical contrast between a lengthened and simple vowel and represents K.km length by postvocalic a in his orthography.

Accent position is distinctive in Kâmkata-vari. Kâmviri has initial- and second-syllable contrasts illustrated by lexical/grammatical pairs; final accent also occurs, but Strand says it is found only in loanwords.

Accented vowels are described as involving anterior laryngeal/vocal-fold tensing and raised pitch, linking Kâmviri lexical accent to a phonetic pitch correlate rather than treating it as an abstract mark only.
Initial /u ü i/ in Kâmviri have homorganic labial or palatal on-glides that are explicitly non-phonemic; Strand contrasts them with phonemic prevocalic v and i/j-type consonants.

In Kâmviri, reduced stricture after consonant onset causes single intervocalic consonants to absorb voicing from surrounding vowels; Strand therefore describes much consonant voicing as positionally determined despite initial voiced/voiceless contrasts.
Utterance-final consonants are fully released and undergo full devoicing in Kâmviri as the larynx lowers and vocal-fold tension relaxes.
/f/ is restricted to loanwords in the comparative Nuristani description; conservative pronunciation replaces it with indigenous /p/.
In Kâmviri, [ž] is not an independent phoneme but the intervocalic or pre-voiced-consonant manifestation of /š/.
Strand calls the phonemic status of y [j] distinct from /i/ doubtful because [j] is the regular manifestation of /i/ before vowels.
Kâmviri has phonemic retroflex approximant ř, while forward flap ṛ is analyzed as an allophone of ṭ in K.km; these statuses differ across Nuristani languages and dialects.
In Kâmviri and Eastern Kâtâ-vari, nasalized retroflex approximant ň phonemically contrasts with retroflex nasal stop ṇ; the cognate sound in Western Kâtâ-vari is ř after loss of nasalization.
The voiceless retroflex lateral affricate-like phone [λ̣] in Kâmviri is analyzed phonemically as the cluster /ṭl/, not as a unit segment.

A dental consonant cannot surface before an apico-alveolar obstruent or nasal without place assimilation: the dental automatically backs to alveolar, making the sequence uniformly alveolar. Retroflex-to-dental sequences are permitted without the reverse adjustment.
Kâmviri /k/ has an intervocalic flapped approximant/spirant-like allophone [ɣ̞].

Loan-only x, ǧ and q are nativized in conservative speech as k, g and k respectively; Arabic-loan pharyngeals ḥ, ˁ and loan h/glottal stop are omitted in conservative pronunciation rather than integrated as native contrasts.

section: Intonation; Table 5 Terminal Intonational Contours in Kâmviri
claim: Kâmviri has a described system of terminal pitch contours distinguishing declaration, information request, emphatic contrast, supplication, explanatory request, regret and continuation; Strand notes this intonation system has been closely studied specifically in K.km.

Open transition/juncture, which blocks normal within-word articulatory overlap, is phonemic in at least Kâmkata-vari; Strand separately marks close, syncopated, accentual, lexical and broken transitions.

Expressive lengthening is salient in Kâmviri: pre-accentual consonant lengthening marks augmentation, accented-vowel lengthening with rising pitch can mark diminution, and a small set uses a two-peaked lengthened vowel for exaggeration.
